Replies to letter of February 4, 1975, Sheldon Meyers (EPA) to John Giacomini (NSF)
p. 1. General Comments, paragraph 2 - Radiological study to be incorporated into the project plan.
Reply. The RISP core samples will be made available to the general scientific community for specific projects. Although many investigators have already expressed interest in analyzing the cores for various physical and chemical properties, no one has yet proposed a study for radionuclides. The RISP office will attempt to contact appropriate investigators to develop a project for this study. The attached sheets indicate the types of studies which are currently planned for the ice cores obtained as part of RISP.
p. 2 Specific Comments, paragraph 1 - Uncontrolled release of hydrocarbons to the environment due to sediment drilling operations.
Reply. During the 1974-1975 Antarctic field season, a long seismic refraction study was made on the Ross Ice Shelf in the vicinity of the proposed drill site. The results of that study are still incomplete, but preliminary values of sediment thickness at the sea bottom at that location are up to 2 kilometers, with a better average of 1.5 kilometers. Structure in the sediment layers was not defined, so it is unknown whether any 'traps' exist that might contain oil or gas. Data are still forthcoming from the refraction study, so we hope to have at least some idea of sub-tottom structure before the drilling begins in 1975-1976.
In any event, precautions will be taken to monitor the sediment cores as they are brought up so that gas analyses can be made with a chromotograph. We have been advised by a geochemist to "... analyze the gases from the muds for hydrocarbons methane through hexane. If appreciable amounts of hydrocarbons heavier than methane are present, say 10% or more of the total hydrocarbons, it suggests that gas is seeping from a deeper accumulation. Consequently, if you have continuous gas shows, and these gases contain the ethane plus hydrocarbons, I would shift to another drill site before going too deep."
In other words, we plan to avoid the problem before it occurs, rather than trying to solve it after it occurs. The same source of the above information mentioned that methane might be encountered nearly continuously in the near surface, "but if it is encountered all the way down the hole, I would abandon the site before going much beyond 300 ft."
If substantial hydrocarbons are encountered, or released, the hole would be plugged and abandoned, as mentioned on p. 31 of the Draft Environmental Statement.
